title: Mesh and geometry views: is the grid adequate?
summary: A picture of the whole computational mesh and a zoom at the wall that shows the first-cell height and the growth of the cells. It lets you judge resolution where the flow changes fastest.

media.alt: Two panels: the whole O-grid mesh around a circular body, and a zoom at the wall showing very small first cells, an orange frame and an annotation of the first-cell height.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the grid adequate?
read_the_figure.axes: No numeric axes: both panels are in physical coordinates scaled by the body diameter (equal aspect). Left: the whole O-grid, 72 by 22 cells. Right: the zoom at the wall, with the first-cell height annotated.
look_at: Are the cells small at the wall and larger away from it (clustering)?
What is the first-cell height and the growth ratio quoted in the zoom title and annotation?
Do cells stay close to square, or are they very stretched?
Is the zoom marked on the full mesh (the orange box)?
read_the_figure.proves: It shows that the grid is dense where gradients are large, and what resolution the wall layer has. It does not show that the result is grid independent: that needs F10.8.
if_wrong: Uniform cells to the wall: the boundary layer is under-resolved.
Large jumps in cell size (growth ratio well above 1.2): numerical error and poor quality.
No zoom or no scale: the viewer cannot judge the wall resolution.

terms.meaning: The set of cells into which the domain is divided for a numerical solution.
Structured mesh that wraps around a body in rings, here a cylinder.
Height of the cell next to the wall, Delta y_1, which sets y+.
Ratio of the height of a layer to the one below it; 1.1 to 1.3 is typical.
Putting small cells where the solution varies fast.

remember: Wall layer: cells small at the wall, growing outward with ratio r.
Sum of N layers: delta = Delta y_1 (r^N - 1) / (r - 1).
Quote Delta y_1 in units of D or metres, and y+.
A mesh picture shows quality, not accuracy.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Lines are the mesh edges; a filled teal disc is the body. The orange box on the left marks the region enlarged at right, with an orange frame and a dotted leader line. The annotation names the first-cell height. Equal aspect ratio keeps cells their true shape.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A mesh is geometry and the reader needs to see geometry. The full view shows topology and overall clustering. The zoom is needed because the wall cell is 1000 times smaller than the body, and invisible at full scale. Marking the zoom region and annotating the first cell connect the two views and give a number the reader can use in the y+ estimate.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: How is the resolution distributed? In the full mesh the rings crowd toward the disc and spread out toward the outer boundary, 72 cells around and 22 radially. Q2: What is the first-cell height? The annotation gives 1.6e-3 D, a thousandth of the diameter, with a growth ratio 1.45 as the zoom title says. Q3: What do you check next? The growth ratio of 1.45 is high compared with 1.1 to 1.3, so the stretching rate of the layer should be reduced or the layer count raised; and Delta y_1 should be converted into y+ for the Reynolds number of the case.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Zoom insets at walls: the box and dotted line tie the zoom to the full mesh. Without the zoom the wall resolution, which is the quantity that matters, cannot be seen.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A pretty mesh can still give a wrong answer: smooth shapes do not prove accuracy. Grid lines are drawn the same width everywhere, so a dense mesh appears as a grey wash that hides the structure. Cells viewed in 2D may be badly skewed in 3D. If the zoom is not to scale (only the first-cell height is labelled), the growth ratio is hard to check. Orthogonality and aspect ratio are not shown.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Colour the cells by a quality metric (aspect ratio, skewness). Plot cell height against wall distance. A table of mesh statistics (cells, y+ range, maximum growth ratio) is compact.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a third panel of the cell height against layer number, with the quoted growth ratio as a line.

steps.note: For Delta y_1 = 1 mm, r = 1.2, N = 10 this is 25.96 mm.

steps.note: A flat-plate estimate, rough for a cylinder; used only to choose the first cell.

worked.title: First-cell height for y+ = 1 at Re = 1e5
worked.problem: A body of diameter D = 1 m in a flow of 1 m/s with nu = 1e-5 m^2/s (Re = 1e5). Estimate Delta y_1 for y+ = 1, and the y+ delivered by the render's Delta y_1 = 1.6e-3 D.

solution.text: First cell for y+ = 1, and the y+ at 1.6e-3 m.

worked.answer: y+ = 1 needs about 0.2 mm (2e-4 D); the render's 1.6e-3 D gives y+ of about 8 at this Re: neither wall-resolved nor in the wall-function range.

analyze.q: What would you do if a growth ratio of 1.45 produced a visible jump in cell size?
The mesh looks good. Why is that not evidence that the result is grid independent?

evaluate.hint: What numbers would you ask for?

Make the version for y+ = 1 and for y+ = 50 and compare the cell counts.

checks.q: Why is there a zoom at the wall?
checks.hint: Compare the first-cell height with the body size.
checks.answer: The wall cell is far too small to see in the full view and it controls y+.

checks.q: Delta y_1 = 1 mm, r = 1.2, N = 10 layers. Total thickness?
The mesh has 72 cells around the cylinder. What is lost?
checks.hint: Think of the resolution of the wake.
checks.answer: 72 cells give 5 degrees each; the separation point and the wake structure may be under-resolved, so check against a finer mesh.
